title: 25 Years After 9/11, What Are We Failing to Imagine Now?
gist: Clarke and Broekaert argue the counterterrorism community's current 'failure of imagination' is not ignorance of drones, generative AI, 3D printing or crypto, but an inability to imagine them combined — and they flag that open-weight AI models let violent actors gain capability with no leakage, while noting most real-world attacks still use knives, vehicles and guns.

insights.claim: The operative risk model for terrorist technology is 'and' not 'either/or': encrypted comms plus virtual-currency funding plus 3D-printed drone components plus AI-assisted target selection and pre-programmed attack routes can be combined in a single operation.
insights.speaker: Colin P. Clarke, Clara Broekaert
insights.so_what: Security budgets and regulation organized tool-by-tool systematically underprice combinatorial risk — expect regulatory catch-up across drone, crypto and AI compliance simultaneously.
insights.locator: When we think about terrorists’ using emerging technologies

insights.claim: Barriers to entry for advanced technologies have been appreciably lowered and commercialized over the past decade, so everyday citizens can now acquire and master tools once obtainable only by states.
insights.speaker: Colin P. Clarke, Clara Broekaert
insights.so_what: The state-to-individual capability diffusion is the core driver of counter-drone, content-moderation and detection spending — a durable demand theme for security tech vendors.
insights.quote: everyday citizens can now acquire and master tools once obtainable only by states

insights.claim: Crashing an explosive-laden drone into a dense Western crowd is described as not a difficult feat, and the authors say it is surprising such an attack has not yet succeeded — several disrupted plots were near fruition and would likely have hit their targets.
insights.speaker: Colin P. Clarke, Clara Broekaert
insights.so_what: An un-priced discontinuous event risk for public venues, insurance and event operators; counter-UAS procurement is the direct beneficiary if it materializes.
insights.quote: Indeed, it is surprising we have not yet seen a successful attack along these lines.
insights.locator: Orchestrating a terror attack using a drone

insights.claim: Weaponized drones have already spread across a wide roster of non-state actors — Hezbollah (since 2006), Hamas, the Houthis, the Islamic State, AQAP, the PKK, Iraqi Shia militias, and actors in Pakistan, Syria and Venezuela — and are now used in combined-arms maneuvers, not just sporadic attacks.
insights.speaker: Colin P. Clarke, Clara Broekaert
entities: al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula
insights.so_what: Drone capability is already globally diffused among non-state actors; assume any regional conflict now includes an aerial threat vector when pricing shipping, energy and infrastructure risk.
insights.locator: Terrorist groups have already used drones successfully

insights.claim: The Russia-Ukraine war has expanded the boundaries of what is possible with drones, functioning as a live R&D lab whose techniques propagate to non-state actors.
insights.speaker: Colin P. Clarke, Clara Broekaert
insights.so_what: Battlefield drone innovation diffuses downward — Ukraine-proven tactics are a forward indicator of Western domestic security requirements.

themes.theme: Generative and open-weight AI as attacker uplift

insights.claim: Generative AI has already featured in several terrorist plots and attacks including on U.S. soil, used organizationally for propaganda by Islamic State Khorasan Province and operationally by Boko Haram.
insights.speaker: Colin P. Clarke, Clara Broekaert
insights.so_what: Concrete misuse cases strengthen the case for AI liability and safety regulation aimed at misuse rather than existential risk — a compliance-cost vector for model providers.
insights.locator: Although only recently commercialized, generative AI

insights.claim: Lone actors are using AI chatbots for bomb-building instructions, operational security tips, and iterative red-teaming conversations to refine tactics, techniques and procedures.
insights.speaker: Colin P. Clarke, Clara Broekaert
insights.so_what: Chat-based red-teaming is a specific, documentable misuse pattern that regulators and plaintiffs can point to — raises model-provider legal exposure.
insights.locator: There have been myriad examples of AI being used by lone terrorists

insights.claim: Open-weight AI models are singled out as the sharpest risk because as they become more capable they can be used by terrorists 'with no leakage' — i.e., without leaving the detection trail that hosted models generate.
insights.speaker: Colin P. Clarke, Clara Broekaert
insights.so_what: The strongest policy argument yet for restricting open-weight releases; a regulatory tail risk for open-source model strategies and a relative advantage for closed API providers.
insights.quote: especially as open-weight AI models become more capable and can be used by terrorists and violent extremists with no leakage

insights.claim: The AI safety community's focus on existential risk is a misallocation — violent non-state actor exploitation deserves serious resources and interventions.
insights.speaker: Colin P. Clarke, Clara Broekaert
insights.so_what: Signals where AI regulation is actually heading — misuse and abuse enforcement, not frontier capability caps.
insights.quote: While the AI safety community predominantly focuses on existential risks, violent non-state actors’ exploitation deserves serious resources and interventions too

insights.claim: AI cuts both ways operationally: terrorists' use of chatbots for planning has already become a source of intelligence collection and plot disruption for law enforcement.
insights.speaker: Colin P. Clarke, Clara Broekaert
insights.so_what: Creates a durable government demand for model-provider data cooperation — expect institutionalized law-enforcement channels into AI platforms.
insights.quote: terrorists’ use of chatbots for operational planning has already become a method of intelligence gathering and, ultimately, plot disruption by law enforcement
insights.locator: And technology is a two-way street

insights.claim: AI is already embedded in the counterterrorism stack: machine learning identifies propaganda for hashing, text/speech/vision classifiers filter millions of multilingual posts, ranking models demote borderline content, and the same infrastructure handles CCTV object detection, financial-flow anomaly detection and rapid search of seized documents.
insights.speaker: Colin P. Clarke, Clara Broekaert
insights.so_what: A concrete, funded government AI use case — surveillance and moderation infrastructure is a less cyclical AI revenue pool than consumer applications.
insights.locator: Advances in artificial intelligence could prove promising

themes.theme: The internet as the enabling layer

insights.claim: The internet is the pervasive facilitator without which none of the other technologies would be adopted — it is the 'leitmotif' of terrorist technology uptake, replacing the physical training-camp model the 9/11 hijackers required.
insights.speaker: Colin P. Clarke, Clara Broekaert
insights.so_what: Platform regulation is the highest-leverage intervention point, which is why content-moderation compliance costs keep rising for social and messaging companies.
insights.quote: Terrorist use of the internet is the leitmotif in terrorists adopting technology.
insights.locator: Virtual currencies are used as terrorist groups solicit

insights.claim: The Salafi jihadist threat in the West is now largely driven by individuals who have never set foot in a conflict theater and never received sustained in-person attack-planning guidance.
insights.speaker: Colin P. Clarke, Clara Broekaert
insights.so_what: Travel-based detection — the infrastructure built post-2014 — is structurally mismatched to the current threat, meaning detection gaps persist despite heavy spending.
insights.quote: the Salafi jihadist terrorist threat landscape in the West is largely driven by individuals who have never set foot in a conflict theater
insights.locator: Not only has the internet democratized access

insights.claim: Counterterrorism travel-denial infrastructure has been genuinely effective — integrated fingerprinting, iris scans, latent-print forensics on bomb fragments, machine-readable passports and harmonized passenger name records have significantly narrowed terrorist mobility.
insights.speaker: Colin P. Clarke, Clara Broekaert
insights.so_what: Demonstrates where security investment actually produced returns — biometric and data-fusion infrastructure, a template governments will extend to other domains.

themes.theme: Shiny object syndrome: simple methods still dominate

insights.claim: Despite the technology narrative, attacks and disrupted plots in the West in recent years rely on simple methods — stabbings, vehicle ramming and shootings are the most commonly executed attacks, largely by lone actors radicalized online.
insights.speaker: Colin P. Clarke, Clara Broekaert
insights.so_what: Guard against over-allocating security budget to exotic tech threats; the base rate of harm still comes from low-tech, high-frequency attacks.

insights.claim: Technology augments rather than replaces simple attack methods: the New Orleans New Year's Day 2025 attacker used smart glasses for reconnaissance months in advance but executed with vehicle ramming and a firearm, and Islamic State-inspired individuals in Italy used a chatbot to learn where to strike someone to cause paralysis.
insights.speaker: Colin P. Clarke, Clara Broekaert
insights.so_what: The detectable signal shifts to the planning phase — consumer device and chatbot telemetry becomes the surveillance frontier, with attendant privacy-policy consequences.
insights.locator: This does not mean that these simple methods

insights.claim: Shiny object syndrome afflicts the counterterrorism apparatus too — community interventions and deep human cultural knowledge remain effective and should not be supplanted by technology where inappropriate.
insights.speaker: Colin P. Clarke, Clara Broekaert
insights.so_what: A caution against assuming security budgets flow unconditionally to tech vendors; human-program spending retains its claim.
insights.locator: Shiny object syndrome also plagues the counterterrorism apparatus

themes.theme: The imagination failure is structural and repeatable

insights.claim: The 9/11 'failure of imagination' was not an information gap — more than 130 attempted hijackings occurred in the U.S. between 1968 and 1972, and Brian Michael Jenkins had described the exact suicide-hijacking-into-a-building scenario at a 1989 aviation security conference.
insights.speaker: Colin P. Clarke, Clara Broekaert
insights.so_what: Warnings are typically already on the record; the failure is institutional attention allocation — a generalizable lesson for how organizations process known tail risks.
insights.quote: The nightmare of governments is that suicidal terrorists will hijack a commercial airliner and, by killing or replacing its crew, crash into a city or some vital facility.
insights.locator: Terrorists hijacking planes was certainly conceivable

insights.claim: The recurring pattern is that the West's own innovations are continuously repurposed against it — planes in 2001, and now drones, AI and 3D printing.
insights.speaker: Colin P. Clarke, Clara Broekaert
insights.so_what: Every major commercialization wave carries a latent security-cost tail; build that regulatory-response risk into diffusion timelines for new technologies.
insights.quote: Its innovations are continuously misused by terrorists against it.
